title: Washington lets Nvidia sell 879,000 AI chips to Chinese giants linked to the military
summary: Washington permits Nvidia to sell 879,000 AI chips to Chinese tech giants
detailed: Here's a surprising deal unfolding in the US right now.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee, chaired by Republican Brian Mast, has released documents from the US Department of Commerce, and they reveal that the office in charge of export licenses approved, at the end of May, the sale of more than 879,000 artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies.
The same office rejected an order for 610,000 chips destined for Alibaba and another for 508,000 for ByteDance, TikTok's parent company.

As for reactions, Democrat Gregory Meeks accuses the Commerce office of failing to enforce the rules, while Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at the financial firm Bernstein, argues on the contrary that 879,000 chips don't amount to much at Nvidia's scale.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee, chaired by Republican Brian Mast, has released documents from the US Department of Commerce, and they reveal that the office in charge of export licenses approved, at the end of May, the sale of more than 879,000 artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies.

Among the approved buyers are Alibaba and Tencent, two giants that nonetheless appear on the Pentagon's list of "Chinese military companies." That's pretty troubling for an administration that swears it wants to slow down Chinese AI.
Between December and May, Nvidia and AMD filed applications covering 3.4 million chips in total, and about one in four was approved.
Most of them are H200s, a previous-generation Nvidia processor that's still powerful enough to train AI models.
The same office rejected an order for 610,000 chips destined for Alibaba and another for 508,000 for ByteDance, TikTok's parent company.
Two companies named in Nvidia's filings, Maginfra and New Matrix, are even suspected of being smuggling fronts, with empty offices to match, according to the New York Times.

Yet every application filed swore that the risk of diversion to the military was "low."
This surprise green light stems from an arrangement made in December, when Donald Trump authorized the shipment of H200s to "approved customers" in China, on the condition that the US government takes 25% of sales.
The craziest part is that these chips haven't really been delivered.
Beijing is blocking imports on a large scale to boost its local manufacturers, and Nvidia says it has stopped shipping H200s to China.
The situation really doesn't make much sense anymore.
This week, the same Department of Commerce also closed the loophole that let Chinese groups rent computing power in third countries.

As a result, Tencent warns that its capacity will shrink, Alibaba is considering scaling back its 20-gigawatt data center target, and both are now betting on mass-produced Chinese chips by 2027 or 2028.

As for reactions, Democrat Gregory Meeks accuses the Commerce office of failing to enforce the rules, while Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at the financial firm Bernstein, argues on the contrary that 879,000 chips don't amount to much at Nvidia's scale.

Jensen Huang, pushed toward the exit after his relationship with an executive suspected of spying for Beijing, will be heard behind closed doors on December 1, followed by Nvidia's chief legal officer the next day.
We can't wait to hear his side of the story.
